#!/bin/sh
# Set up a boxd pool on a discobox server: make a new boxd API key with the
# boxd CLI, create (or update) a boxd provider named boxd with it, and create a
# pool named boxd on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/boxd-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base ID] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh                                  # provider and pool "boxd", made in nyc
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --region fra                     # the boxd region, which the provider requires
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --base <boxd image or snapshot ID>
#
# Run `boxd login` first: boxd makes API keys only for an interactive session.
# Each run makes a new key, named <name>-<random>. When the provider already
# exists its config is replaced with the new key, keeping its region unless
# --region names one (a region cannot change while the provider has pools), and
# the key it held is left in boxd for you to revoke. Flags the script does not know (--server, --project,
# ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default: discobox on
# PATH) and $BOXD the boxd CLI (default: boxd on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The key is the server's
# alone: the pool's machine authenticates as itself, and is given no key (ADR
# 26-11-11-080 §9). The server seals the key in the provider's row and never
# returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The provider names its region and no endpoint: the driver asks boxd's home
# endpoint for the region's (ListRegions) and makes and lists its machines
# there, while the key exchange and account calls stay at the home endpoint
# (ADR 26-11-15-507 §3).
set -eu

name=boxd
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
boxd=${BOXD:-boxd}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,30p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

for cli in "$boxd" "$discobox"; do
	command -v "$cli" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$cli is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
done
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# A new provider is made in nyc unless --region says otherwise; an existing one
# keeps its region. Decided before a key is made, so a refusal leaves none.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
		if [ -z "$region" ]; then
			echo "provider $name has no region, which boxd now requires; delete it and its pools and run this again (docs/public/boxd.md, Upgrading a provider without a region)" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
	fi
fi
[ -n "$region" ] || region=nyc

suffix=$(od -An -N4 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')
key_name="$name-$suffix"
if ! out=$("$boxd" auth keys create "$key_name" 2>&1); then
	printf '%s\n' "$out" >&2
	echo "boxd did not make a key; run \`boxd login\` and try again" >&2
	exit 1
fi
key=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -oE 'bxd_[A-Za-z0-9_-]+' | head -1 || true)
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	echo "boxd made key $key_name but printed no bxd_ key; revoke it in boxd" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "made boxd API key $key_name" >&2

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
jq -n --arg key "$key" --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: {apiKey: $key, region: $region}} + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "updated provider $name with the new key; revoke the key it held before in boxd" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider create --type boxd --name "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "created provider $name in $region" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
fi
echo "run a discobox on it with: $discobox run --pool $name" >&2

# Set up an archil pool on a discobox server: create (or update) an archil
# provider named archil with an Archil API key, and create a pool named archil
# on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/archil-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base IMAGE] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh                                # provider and pool "archil", in aws-us-east-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --region aws-eu-west-1         # aws-us-east-1, aws-us-west-2 or aws-eu-west-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --base debian:sid              # the public OCI image a fresh VM runs
#
# Archil has no CLI that makes keys: make one in the Archil console and pass it
# in $ARCHIL_API_KEY, or the script asks for it on the terminal without echoing
# it. When the provider already exists its config is replaced with the key,
# keeping its region unless --region names one (a region cannot change while
# the provider has pools). Flags the script does not know (--server,
# --project, ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default:
# discobox on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The server seals the key
# in the provider's row and never returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The server refuses a pool on archil for now: Archil has no machine isolation
# to fence a pool's sandboxes with (docs/public/concepts.md, VM providers). The
# provider is still made, and the pool's refusal is printed as the server says
# it.
set -eu

name=archil
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,28p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

command -v "$discobox" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$discobox is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# An existing provider keeps its region unless --region names one; a new one
# without --region is the driver's default.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
	fi
fi

key=${ARCHIL_API_KEY:-}
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	[ -t 0 ] || { echo "set ARCHIL_API_KEY to an API key from the Archil console" >&2; exit 2; }
	printf 'Archil API key: ' >&2
	stty -echo
	trap 'stty echo' EXIT INT TERM
	IFS= read -r key || true
	stty echo
	trap - EXIT INT TERM
	echo >&2
fi
key=$(printf '%s' "$key" | tr -d '[:space:]')
[ -n "$key" ] || { echo "no Archil API key given" >&2; exit 2; }

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key; the key reaches jq through its environment.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
ARCHIL_API_KEY=REDACTED jq -n --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: ({apiKey: $ENV.ARCHIL_API_KEY} + (if $region == "" then {} else {region: $region} end))}
	 + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "updated provider $name with the key" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider create --type archil --name "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "created provider $name in ${region:-the default region (aws-us-east-1)}" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
elif "$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null; then
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
else
	echo "the server refused pool $name (above); provider $name is kept" >&2
	exit 1
fi

**One thing to know first:** the server currently refuses pools on archil. `docs/public/concepts.md` says this is because Archil has no machine isolation, and the code check is in `server/providers/discovm/provider.go:190`. - **`--base`:** sets the public OCI image a fresh VM runs, e.g. `debian:sid`.

`--server` isn't a flag of the script. It's the `discobox` CLI's global flag for choosing which discobox server to talk to (`cli/internal/cli/root.go:231`). The script doesn't recognise it, so it passes it, along with any other unknown flag, to every `discobox` call it makes.

It takes either an endpoint URL (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:8080`) or the name of a server you've registered with `discobox admin remote`. If you leave it off, the CLI uses `$DISCOBOX_SERVER` if that's set. Otherwise it uses the primary remote, or the local server if you haven't set a primary.

So the `--server http://127.0.0.1:8080` in the example just means "set up the provider and pool on the server at that address." For your usual server, leave it off.

# Encryption Design

`internal/encryption` seals what the server stores encrypted (ADR
26-11-02-902). It is discobox's use of `github.com/discobox-ai/envelope`:
each project's values are sealed with the project's own data key, and data
keys are stored only wrapped by the configured provider.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    config["config.EncryptionSettings (server.yaml encryption:)"] --> new[encryption.New]
    new --> provider["envelope provider: local, awskms, gcpkms, azurekeyvault, vaulttransit"]
    new --> keyring[Keyring]
    keyring --> envelope[envelope.Keyring]
    envelope -- "wrapped data keys" --> keys["store.EncryptionKeys (encryption_keys)"]
    store[internal/store] --> keyring
    auth["auth/sandbox, auth/poolagent"] --> keyring
```

- A `Field` names where a value lives: its scope (a project ID, or
  `ServerScope`), purpose, and resource ID. The scope picks the data key; the
  purpose and resource ID are the associated data, so a value's bytes do not
  open anywhere else. The constructors (`SecretValue`, ...) are the complete
  list of sealed fields; add one here when a column is sealed, and to
  `store.sealedColumns` so startup re-seals it.
- A nil `Keyring` is a server with no provider: values are stored unsealed,
  and a sealed one is an error rather than bytes passed through.
- `Open` reads every form a stored value has: `envelope:v1:`, `discobox:v1:`
  (sealed by a release before data keys with `encryptionKey`, opened with the
  local key or a retired one), and unsealed. `SealForWrite` stores any of
  them in the current format, verifying a sealed one against its field.
- `New` builds every provider from the SDK's own credential chain; Vault and
  OpenBao log in from the configuration. A Kubernetes login is renewed and
  repeated, and a `file:` token read again every 30s, until `Close`. A provider whose key cannot be reached fails
  `New`, so the server never starts on a misconfigured one.
- `encryption.local.key` opens what an earlier release sealed whichever
  provider is configured, so a server can move from `encryptionKey`
  straight to a KMS.
- `previous` adds an unwrap-only provider. The local provider's retired keys
  are unwrap-only too. Startup (`store.PrepareEncryption`) rewraps what
  either wrapped.

## Rules

- A scope's first key is made outside any transaction (`Ensure`): a key
  stored by a transaction that rolls back stays cached and seals values
  nothing can open later.
- Cloud credentials never come from the configuration file.

The key is only ever stored on the server, encrypted, in the provider's row in the server's database. The script and CLI don't keep a copy.

1. **The script** reads `$ARCHIL_API_KEY`, or the hidden prompt, and writes it into a 0600 temp file made by `mktemp`. That file is deleted when the script exits. The key reaches `jq` through its environment, so it never appears on a command line where `ps` could see it.
2. **The CLI** reads that file (`--config @file`) and sends the key to the server in the body of the provider create or update request.
3. **The server** stores it encrypted, per ADR 26-10-31-694:
   - It moves the `driver.apiKey` field out of the provider's plain `config` column and into `encrypted_config`, sealed with the project's data key.
   - That data key is stored only wrapped by the server's encryption provider, set in `server.yaml` under `encryption:`. The options are local key, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault and Vault/OpenBao (`server/internal/encryption/DESIGN.md`).
   - The API never returns the key, and project secrets and agent bindings can't reach it.
   - The server decrypts it only in memory, to call Archil's API.

**One caveat:** if your server has no encryption provider configured, the value is stored as base64 of the plaintext rather than encrypted. I haven't checked how your server is configured. Look for an `encryption:` section in its `server.yaml`.

The variable also stays in your own shell if you exported it. Running it as a one-off prefix, `ARCHIL_API_KEY=key-... scripts/archil-pool.sh`, avoids that.

Yes, and the script now does it. Archil has no API that reports a key's region, but each region has its own control plane, and an invalid key gets a 401 from all three. So without `--region`, the script sends the key to each region's control plane (a sandbox listing, the same call the driver makes) and uses the one region that accepts it.

- **No region accepts the key:** it stops with "no Archil region takes that key".
- **More than one accepts it** (which shouldn't happen): it asks you to pass `--region`.
- **A region gives an unexpected answer** (not success, 401 or 403), or can't be reached: it stops and tells you to pass `--region`, rather than guess.
- **`--region`** still works and skips the check.
- **Existing provider:** it gets the found region along with the new key. The server refuses a region change while the provider has pools, so a mismatched key fails there rather than silently.

The key is passed to `curl` on stdin (`-K -`), so it never appears on a command line. The script also rejects a key containing a quote or backslash, because those would break `curl`'s config syntax.

**Tested so far:** an invalid key gets "no Archil region takes that key", and `--region` builds the right config against a stub `discobox`. **Not tested:** that a valid key is accepted only in its own region. I don't have a real key, so the first real run with yours will be the test. It should print "the key is for aws-…" before creating the provider.

## Create a pool and run a box

```sh
discobox admin pool create boxd --provider boxd
discobox admin pool get boxd
discobox run --pool boxd
```

The pool is ready when `admin pool get` shows it `active`. The first box of a
kind (its harness and setup) provisions from scratch, and takes longest.
Behind it, the pool builds a snapshot of that kind on a machine of its own;
boxes of that kind made once the snapshot is ready start from it. Make the
pool the project's default with `discobox admin pool set-default boxd`.

Before it makes a pool's machine, the server checks the account through
boxd's API: that the key is accepted, that the org has the provider's region
enabled, and that no host-bound secret is in the org or the key owner's
personal scope. The pool fails with the reason if boxd refuses, and waits if
boxd does not answer. A running pool's account is checked again every ten
minutes, which reads the org's machine limit: the pool's `runtime` condition
shows it as `maxMachines`, counting every machine billed to the org, stopped
ones and other members' included. A check that fails then is logged, and the
pool keeps running.

## Snapshots A delivered create starts from a **snapshot** of its plan when the pool has one, and otherwise from its base, provisioning from scratch as above while the snapshot is built behind it ([ADR 26-10-16-423](../docs/adr/26-10-16-423-a-harness-is-a-provisioning-bundle-and-the-agent-provisions-any-box.md) §8, [ADR 26-11-03-986](../docs/adr/26-11-03-986-a-machine-pool-snapshots-a-plan-by-committing-a-vm-it-provisioned-and-shut-down.md); `snapshot.go`, shared by both runtimes). A snapshot is only a cache: the control plane is told what the pool holds and which a box started from ([Reporting](#reporting)) and decides nothing from it, and nothing fails for want of one. A Docker pool's snapshot is a committed image (`snapshotdocker.go`); a machine pool's is a committed disco-vm VM, and only where its driver reports `Capabilities.Commit` ([On a machine pool](#on-a-machine-pool)). ```mermaid flowchart LR create["delivered create"] --> key["plan key: base, project, pool,
agent, pins, features off, provisionEgress"] key -->|"a snapshot of the plan"| snap["start from the snapshot"] key -->|"none"| base["start from the base"] --> ask["build it in the background
(one at a time; a failure waits an hour)"] ask --> build["build box: base + agent layer + pins"] build -->|"exec: discobox-sandbox-agent snapshot, SnapshotPlan on stdin
(provisions, every feature done, cleans, seals)"| stop["stop in order"] stop --> commit["commit"] ``` - **The build is one exec** (`runSnapshotCommand`, through `provisioner.Provision` on both runtimes: a container as `provisioner.ContainerGuest`). The taker starts its box, places the agent, its units and its pins, and runs the agent's `snapshot` command as one blocking exec with the plan on its stdin, whose exit status and stderr are the build's result. The command refuses to seal a box with any feature not done or failed (as `discobox-provision wait` reads it), so no snapshot is committed that is not provisioned whole. The guest never powers itself off: the taker stops the box in order and commits it. - **The key** (`snapshotPlan`) is everything the snapshot holds depends on and nothing of the sandbox: the base (a Docker pool's sandbox base image ID; a machine pool's driver and the base its configuration names), the agent it is placed with and its bundles in order, the features turned off, and the create's `provisionEgress`. Every sandbox of one plan shares one snapshot. - **A build is anonymous.** Its proxy identity is its own (`layout.SnapshotIDPrefix`), with a client certificate, and an asset record of the plan's pins in its own tree, `layout.Root.Snapshot` — never a sandbox's tree, so neither the control plane nor any sandbox sweep sees it — and the egress policy the server sends as `provisionEgress`: every level of ADR 26-10-01-032 but the sandbox's own. Its `agentlayer.SnapshotPlan` names no account, source, secret, gateway, sentinel or credentials endpoint. The material reaper leaves a build's identity alone, since it has no sandbox container to be found by: its material goes with the build, or with the sweep once its container is gone. - **Nothing of the build is committed but what it provisioned.** The plan, which holds the build's client key, is never on a disk: it is the command's stdin. Its proxy material and the agent's record of it are under `/etc/discobox`, which is never on the committed disk either — a Docker build's bind, a VM build's tmpfs the command mounts in systemd's own mount namespace, entering it first where the exec runs in another (boxd's) — and which the command empties before it returns. It empties `machine-id`, removes SSH host keys, gives back the provider's resolver its DNS stub took over (and the record of it), takes the build's proxy CA back out of the trust store, and writes the seal (`agentlayer.SealedFile`): a box made from a snapshot gives itself a new machine ID and SSH host keys when its bootstrap arrives, before anything else, since a boot the pool did not run (boxd's commit boots the disk once more) may have written them again. It removes the agent's start link, so a box made from the snapshot starts its agent when its maker says, as a fresh one does, and the re-execution for the new machine ID never runs under the maker's own systemctl calls. A container inherits its image's labels, so the build carries only its project's and pool's, which every container of the pool carries, and none saying it is a build, which would mark every sandbox started from the snapshot. It is found by its name (`snapshotContainerPrefix`) with those labels: one no build under way holds — left by an agent that stopped mid-build, maybe still running — is swept with its tree and proxy material by the image reclaim, so none provisions on under a policy the pool no longer keeps, and it is removed with its pool by `SyncKnownPools`. - **A build is a start.** On a Docker pool it enters the pool's start gate for its whole length, and a cache clear ends it once the gate is shut ([Clearing the Pool's Caches](#clearing-the-pools-caches)). On either, a clear forgets the plans that failed. - **A plan whose build failed waits an hour** before a create asks again. Its failure is kept in the pool's tree (`snapshot-failures/`), not in memory, so an agent that keeps restarting does not keep building: a JSON record of when, why (the build's error, bounded, its middle elided) and the plan. You can see whether a build is queued or running and when it started, but not how far along it is. Nothing reports progress within a build.

**`discobox admin pool get <pool>`** is the main place to look. It shows a `SNAPSHOTS` summary line (e.g. `1 held, 1 building, 0 failed`) and then one row per snapshot:

```
SNAPSHOT      STATE     WHEN              PLAN                 DETAIL
3f9a1c2e7b04  building  started 4m ago    claude-code@ab12…
```

- `STATE` is one of:
  - `queued`: asked for, but waiting behind another build, since a pool runs one build at a time.
  - `building`: running.
  - `held`: done; DETAIL shows its size, how many boxes use it and when it was last used.
  - `failed`: DETAIL shows the error and when a new create may try again (failed builds wait an hour).
- `-o json` has the full record (`resources.snapshots.building[]` with `requestedAt`/`startedAt`).
- This comes from the pool's resource report, so it refreshes on each report tick rather than live (ADR 26-11-17-316, `cli/internal/cli/pool_snapshots.go`).

**`discobox admin pool logs <pool> --follow`** shows the pool agent's own log lines: `building a snapshot`, then `built a snapshot … took=…` or the failure with its error (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/snapshot.go:218-243`). That tells you when a build starts and ends, but nothing in between.

**`discobox ls`** has a `STARTED FROM` column, which says whether each box started from a snapshot (and which one) or from the base.

The build itself is one blocking exec of the sandbox agent's `snapshot` command. Only its exit status and stderr come back, and only as the result, so feature-by-feature provisioning progress isn't streamed anywhere. Meanwhile the box that triggered the build is provisioning from scratch on its own, and its progress shows normally, since that's the box's own provisioning rather than the snapshot's. Adding per-step progress would mean streaming the exec's output, or a progress field in the `building` record.

There's no CLI command that streams a snapshot build's log. The pool agent only gets the build's output when it finishes: the tail of stderr, and only on failure. That's what appears in `admin pool get` and `admin pool logs`.

While a build runs, the log lives inside the build box. The build provisions each feature with the same runner a normal box uses, and each feature writes to `/var/log/discobox/provision/<feature>.log` (`sandbox-agent/provision/box.go:15`). To watch it, get a shell in the build box:

**Docker pool:** the build is a container on the pool host called `discobox-snapshot-<poolID>-<id>`.
```sh
discobox admin pool console <pool>          # root shell on the pool host, with its Docker socket
docker ps --filter name=discobox-snapshot-
docker exec -it <container> sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log'
```

**VM pool (boxd):** the build is a machine whose name starts with `snap-` followed by the first 24 characters of the plan key (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/machinesnapshot.go:52`). Find it in `boxd machine list`, then:
```sh
boxd machine exec <snap-machine> -- sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log'
```
`discobox admin pool console <pool>` also works here: on a remote driver it gives a login shell on the pool's machine. I haven't confirmed that boxd shows the build machine under exactly that `snap-` name, so check the list.

Inside the box, `/run/discobox/provision` (the status file `discobox-provision wait` reads) shows which features are done, running or failed.

Two catches:
- Grab the logs before the build ends. On success the box is stopped and committed; on failure it's removed. Afterwards, only the stderr tail in the `failed` row of `admin pool get` is left.
- The box that triggered the build is provisioning the same features from scratch at the same time, and its logs are easier to reach: `discobox exec <box> -- tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log`. It's usually the quickest way to see what the snapshot is doing, though it's a separate run, not the build's own output.

If you want this in the product, the natural fix would be to stream the build exec's output into the pool agent's log, or expose the build box's feature logs through `admin pool get`. I can sketch either.

content.text:
I filed it as **https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox/issues/1597**, labelled `type/feature`, `area/cli`, `area/pool-agent` and `priority/medium`.

The issue asks for:
- **A listing of builds:** for example `discobox admin box ls --snapshots`, or a flag on `discobox ls`, showing each running build's pool, plan key, state and what it runs in. It would be read from the pool's report, because builds deliberately have no sandbox row (ADR 26-11-17-316).
- **Progress:** each build's per-feature provisioning status (state, step, error), the way a box already reports it, so you can see where it's stuck without a shell.
- **Logs and a shell:** following a build's feature logs and running commands in it through the CLI, without provider credentials. This matters most on archil, where the pool's console can't reach the build machine.
- **Optionally, keeping a failed build:** leaving a failed build's box around for a while so its logs can still be read.

It's done when all of that works while a build runs, on a Docker pool and on an archil or boxd pool.

Your current build is likely hitting **#1585**, which is already open: "An archil pool's snapshot build never reaches the pool". The build machine's proxy bridge can't reach the pool because it has no edge path. That issue describes builds sitting in `building` for 30 minutes, which fits what we're seeing. The issue only says "likely", since nothing in discobox could confirm it, which is the gap #1597 is about.

</pasted_content id="2d4b">

That log line confirms it: this build is stuck on **#1585**.

It's the same error #1585 records. The build machine's proxy bridge tries to reach the pool by resolving `7302-<pool host>.prod-aws-us-west-2-green.archil.app`. It asks `8.8.8.8` and `1.1.1.1` through the guest's resolver (`169.254.53.53`), and both time out because the pool's fence blocks the guest's DNS. A normal box on this pool doesn't need DNS here: it's given the edge path and credentials URL. The build machine's `bridge.json` doesn't get them, so it can never reach the pool proxy, and it can't fetch bundles or finish provisioning.

What this means for you:
- **This build won't finish.** It stays `building` until it times out. After a failure, the plan waits an hour before a new box asks for another build.
- **Boxes still work.** New boxes keep starting from the base and provisioning from scratch, as `sbx_74pw9ze1vesshxzb` did. They just don't get the snapshot speed-up.
- **The fix is #1585,** which is already `status/in-progress`. The build machine needs the same edge placement a box gets.

This also adds to #1585: it now reproduces in `aws-us-west-2`, not just `us-east-1`. The pool's region came from the key, so `archil-pool.sh` chose `aws-us-west-2`. Want me to add this log line to #1585 as a comment?
